extracted.intended_audience: press officers, science communicators, institutional PR staff, and journalists
extracted.subtask_description: A rubric for crafting science press releases that are likely to be picked up by quality news outlets: balances scientific accuracy/caveats with journalistic clarity, provides access and visuals, and communicates uncertainty appropriately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Asymmetry of professional incentives
rubrics_metrics.description: Scientists are rewarded for caveat-rich rigor; journalists for clear narratives. The release must satisfy both: sufficient caveat to defend to scientists, sufficient narrative clarity to be usable by journalists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write releases that foreground a clear, usable narrative while retaining enough caveats and methodological detail that scientist-sources will accept the representation. Avoid stripping all uncertainty for the sake of a tidy story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Translation function (bilingual PR writer)
rubrics_metrics.description: The release is a translation artifact. The PR-officer should be a bilingual writer fluent in scientific accuracy and journalistic style.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compose copy that accurately renders technical claims in plain language and that anticipates journalists' needs (hooks, leads, quotable soundbites) without misrepresenting the science.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independent expert availability
rubrics_metrics.description: Pickup-worthy releases supply contact info for at least one independent expert who can comment to journalists with appropriate distance from the issuer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide names, affiliations, phone/email and preferably a brief note on the expert's independence; make third-party voices available to validate or contextualize findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct-author availability windows
rubrics_metrics.description: Releases should commit to scientist availability for a defined window (e.g., 'Dr. Y available for media calls between 9 a.m.–5 p.m. ET on [date]').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give explicit times/dates when authors or spokespeople can be reached to facilitate timely interviews and avoid missed opportunities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Materials for the visual journalist
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide photos of researchers, lab images, sample animations — visual material is often a chronic gap in scientist-supplied releases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include high-quality, captioned images, video, or animations and make clear usage/credit terms; anticipate visual story needs to increase pickup.

rubrics_metrics.name: Background packets (FAQ-style)
rubrics_metrics.description: A FAQ-style backgrounder for the topic (separate from the release) increases pickup by giving the reporter context to ground the new finding in.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supply a succinct backgrounder or FAQ that explains methods, prior literature, technical terms, limitations, and relevance so reporters can quickly situate the new result.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explicit uncertainty disclosure (quantitative)
rubrics_metrics.description: For new or controversial science, the release should state uncertainty quantitatively (95% CI, range of estimates) rather than rhetorically ('possibly', 'might').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whenever feasible present numeric confidence intervals, effect-size ranges, or probability statements instead of vague qualifiers; this improves accuracy and reduces misinterpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consensus-vs-frontier signal
rubrics_metrics.description: Make clear whether the finding is at the consensus core, at the frontier, or in active controversy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Signal whether results confirm well-established knowledge, extend it slightly, or challenge it—outlets serving informed audiences screen for this distinction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Replication and prior-evidence context
rubrics_metrics.description: Anchor the new result in prior literature ('This is the [N]th study to find...', 'First study to test [intervention] in [population]').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State how the new work relates to existing evidence—whether it replicates, contradicts, or is novel—and cite key prior studies to help reporters assess significance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dissent acknowledgment
rubrics_metrics.description: Releases on contested findings should acknowledge dissenting views; pretending unanimity invites correction stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mention alternative interpretations, competing studies, or methodological critiques where relevant rather than presenting a false consensus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Range of plausible outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: For predictive findings (climate, epidemiology, economic forecast), the release should report the range, not the central estimate alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide best-case/worst-case or probability-distribution information so reporters can convey uncertainty rather than a single deterministic forecast.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time-horizon clarity
rubrics_metrics.description: "By 2050" or 'within 5 years' or 'in this decade' — be explicit about the time horizon of any predicted effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specify concrete timeframes for predicted effects or impacts to avoid vague phrasing that misleads audiences about timing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pickup-worthiness: respect both communities
rubrics_metrics.description: Pickup at quality outlets correlates with visible respect for both communities — sufficient scientific care to satisfy scientist sources; sufficient narrative clarity, visuals, and access to satisfy journalist users.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance rigor (transparent methods, uncertainty, expert context) with journalistic usability (clear lead, visuals, accessible quotes, and availability). Controlled uncertainty disclosure (with quantified ranges) increases pickup at quality outlets and reduces correction risk.
